title: Break-even analysis with a worked calculation for Garden maintenance and clean-ups
audience: Garden maintenance business owners who set prices or plan monthly revenue, including solo operators.
learningOutcomes: Classify the costs of a garden maintenance business as fixed or variable
Calculate monthly break-even revenue from fixed costs and a variable cost percentage
Explain why conflicting break-even figures must be reconciled before any of them is used

instruction.heading: What break-even means
instruction.body: Break-even revenue is the amount of sales that covers all costs exactly, so profit is zero. Below that level a garden business loses money. Above it, each further dollar of sales adds to profit. The figure is useful for setting prices, deciding when to add a crew member and checking whether a new upkeep route can pay for itself. It is a planning tool, and its answer is only as good as the costs and percentages behind it.

instruction.heading: Split costs into fixed and variable
instruction.body: Fixed costs do not change with the number of jobs in a month. They include the van or trailer loan, insurance, phone and software subscriptions, storage rent and registration. Variable costs move with each job. They include green-waste disposal, fuel, consumables, blades and string, subcontractor fees and the card payment fees charged on each sale. Express variable cost as a percentage of sales: divide the variable cost in a period by the sales in the same period. ANZ defines the two cost types and warns that costs must be covered to avoid running at a loss (ANZ, 21 February 2025). Check the percentage across at least three months before relying on it, because one unusual month can mislead.

instruction.heading: The formula
instruction.body: Break-even revenue equals fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage. One minus the variable percentage is the contribution margin: the share of each dollar of sales left to cover fixed costs. Use the variable percentage as a decimal, so 25 per cent becomes 0.25. The contribution margin of a 25 per cent variable cost is then 0.75 (Xero Australia, 23 July 2026).

instruction.heading: Work the calculation in order
instruction.body: Write the inputs first, each with its source, period and date. Compute the contribution margin, then divide the fixed costs by it. Convert the result into a number of jobs at your average job price, and round up to whole jobs, because a part job does not cover costs on its own (Xero Australia, 23 July 2026). Check that the average price is what you actually charge, excluding GST if you are registered. GST is added to the price once a business is registered, and the threshold is $75,000 of GST turnover (ATO, 14 September 2026). Confirm the GST position with the ATO or an accountant. Do not use a vendor's price range as your average, because a range does not show your own job mix.

instruction.heading: Reconcile before you use any figure
instruction.body: When two figures disagree, go back to the inputs. Confirm that each fixed cost is a monthly amount and not an annual one. Confirm that the variable percentage is a share of sales and not of cost. Confirm that the output is revenue and not profit, and that the price is stated on the same GST basis as the sales. Then write down the reconciled figure with its inputs and drop the others. A figure that cannot be checked should not be used to set a price.

procedure: List every monthly cost and label each one fixed or variable.
Work out variable cost as a percentage of sales for the same period, and check it across at least three months.
Calculate one minus the variable percentage to find the contribution margin.
Divide monthly fixed costs by the contribution margin to get break-even revenue.
Divide break-even revenue by your average job price, excluding GST if registered, to get the number of jobs needed each month, rounded up.
Compare any other break-even figure with your result, reconcile the inputs, and keep only the reconciled figure.

workedExamples.situation: Hypothetical figures, invented for this lesson and not market data: a two-person garden maintenance business has fixed costs of $2,200 a month (van loan, insurance, phone and software), variable costs of 25 per cent of sales (green-waste disposal, consumables, fuel and card fees) and an average job price of $150 excluding GST.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How many jobs must the business complete each month to break even, and what should it check before setting prices?
workedExamples.reasoning: The contribution margin is 1 minus 0.25, which is 0.75. Break-even revenue is $2,200 divided by 0.75, which is $2,933.33 a month. At $150 a job that is 19.56 jobs, so the business needs 20 jobs to cover its costs. Each job contributes $112.50 ($150 multiplied by 0.75) towards fixed costs. Check the arithmetic: 19 jobs contribute $2,137.50, which is short of $2,200, and 20 jobs contribute $2,250. Before setting prices, the business checks that the 25 per cent includes disposal and every other variable cost, that $2,200 is a monthly figure, and that $150 is the average price charged, excluding GST.

equipmentAndPpe: Cost list for the last three months
Job invoice log with dates and GST status

commonErrors.prevention: Convert every cost to the same period before dividing, and label each input with its period.

commonErrors.error: Using variable cost as a share of cost instead of a share of sales
commonErrors.prevention: Divide variable cost by sales for the same period, and write the denominator beside the percentage.

commonErrors.error: Copying a break-even figure from a plan without its inputs
commonErrors.prevention: Recalculate from your own inputs and record the source and date of each input before using the result.
Round up to whole jobs, because a part job does not cover costs on its own.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business planning only. This lesson gives no tax or accounting advice. Check the tax treatment of costs and GST registration with a registered tax agent or qualified accountant.
This lesson does not grant any licence, registration or authority.

qualityStandard: Every break-even figure shows its fixed costs, variable percentage, period, GST basis and source.
Two figures that disagree are reconciled before either one is used in a plan or a price.
documentationEvidence: Cost list split into fixed and variable, with source and date
Reconciliation note wherever two figures disagree
summary: Break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage.
Use one period and one GST basis throughout the calculation.
Recalculate from your own inputs. Do not copy another plan's break-even figure.

knowledgeChecks.question: Break-even revenue is calculated as:
options: Fixed costs divided by (1 minus the variable cost percentage)
Fixed costs multiplied by the variable cost percentage
Sales minus fixed costs, shown as a percentage of the cost

knowledgeChecks.question: Fixed costs are $2,200 a month and variable costs are 25% of sales. What is the monthly break-even revenue?
Two sources give different break-even figures for the same garden business. What is the right response?
options: Use the larger figure to be safe and ignore the smaller figure entirely
Recalculate from your own costs and check each source's inputs before using any figure
Average the two figures together and quote the result to the client today
Use the price list alone and skip the break-even check and rely on the owner's gut feel

sourceReferences: Xero Australia, 'Break-even point formula' glossary entry, https://www.xero.com/au/glossary/break-even-point-formula/, dated 23 July 2026. Supports: contribution margin is price minus variable cost; break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by the contribution ratio; job counts are rounded up to whole jobs.

ANZ, 'Setting the right price for your product or service', https://www.anz.com.au/business/business-hub/starting-business/start/setting-the-right-price-for-your-product-or-service/, dated 21 February 2025, last modified 22 July 2025. Supports: definitions of fixed and variable costs; costs must be covered to avoid operating at a loss.

ATO, 'Registering for GST', https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/gst-excise-and-indirect-taxes/gst/registering-for-gst, last updated 14 September 2026. Supports: GST turnover threshold of $75,000; GST is added to the price once registered.
